claim: Deletion of FICD abolished detectable modification of endogenous BiP in mammalian cells.
source: We report that deletion of FICD, a gene encoding an ER-localized AMPylating enzyme, abolished detectable modification of endogenous BiP enhancing ER buffering of unfolded protein stress in mammalian cells
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of FICD enhanced ER buffering of unfolded protein stress in mammalian cells.
source: We report that deletion of FICD, a gene encoding an ER-localized AMPylating enzyme, abolished detectable modification of endogenous BiP enhancing ER buffering of unfolded protein stress in mammalian cells
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing attenuated UPR activation in FICD-/- cells.

claim: Deregulated FICD activity had the opposite effect on ER buffering of unfolded protein stress compared to FICD deletion.
source: We report that deletion of FICD, a gene encoding an ER-localized AMPylating enzyme, abolished detectable modification of endogenous BiP enhancing ER buffering of unfolded protein stress in mammalian cells, whilst deregulated FICD activity had the opposite effect.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by data showing UPR activation upon expression of constitutively active FICD.

claim: FICD AMPylated BiP to completion on a single residue, Thr518, in vitro.
source: In vitro, FICD AMPylated BiP to completion on a single residue, Thr518.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data and mutagenesis experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: AMPylation increased in a strictly FICD-dependent manner as the flux of proteins entering the ER was attenuated in vivo.
source: AMPylation increased, in a strictly FICD-dependent manner, as the flux of proteins entering the ER was attenuated in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing increased BiP modification upon cycloheximide treatment in wildtype but not FICD-/- cells.

claim: Thr518 AMPylation enhanced peptide dissociation from BiP 6-fold in vitro.
source: In vitro, Thr518 AMPylation enhanced peptide dissociation from BiP 6-fold and abolished stimulation of ATP hydrolysis by J-domain cofactor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Thr518 AMPylation abolished stimulation of ATP hydrolysis by J-domain cofactor in vitro.
source: In vitro, Thr518 AMPylation enhanced peptide dissociation from BiP 6-fold and abolished stimulation of ATP hydrolysis by J-domain cofactor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: BiP affects protein folding homeostasis and the response to ER stress.
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized Hsp70 chaperone BiP affects protein folding homeostasis and the response to ER stress.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Reversible inactivating covalent modification of BiP is believed to contribute to the balance between chaperones and unfolded ER proteins.
source: Reversible inactivating covalent modification of BiP is believed to contribute to the balance between chaperones and unfolded ER proteins, but the nature of this modification has so far been hinted at indirectly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is based on prior literature cited in the introduction.

claim: The UPR regulates the abundance of BiP transcriptionally.
source: The UPR regulates the abundance of BiP transcriptionally (Chang et al., 1989; Kozutsumi et al., 1988), but this is a latent homeostatic process manifesting over hours and days.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transcriptional regulation of BiP abundance is a latent homeostatic process manifesting over hours and days.
source: The UPR regulates the abundance of BiP transcriptionally (Chang et al., 1989; Kozutsumi et al., 1988), but this is a latent homeostatic process manifesting over hours and days.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on established knowledge about transcriptional regulation kinetics.

claim: BiP's oligomeric state changes on a much shorter time scale than transcriptional regulation, with fewer oligomers present as levels of unfolded protein increase.
source: On a much shorter time scale BiP's oligomeric state is observed to change, with fewer oligomers present as levels of unfolded protein increase.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The architecture of BiP oligomers is consistent with their role as a rapidly accessible repository of inactive BiP.
source: The architecture of BiP oligomers is consistent with their role as a rapidly accessible repository of inactive BiP that the cell may draw upon in short notice to cope with rapid fluctuations in unfolded protein load (Preissler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: BiP is subject to activity-dependent post-translational modification(s) reflected in transfer of metabolic label from intracellular pools of tritiated adenosine and 32P phosphate onto BiP.
source: BiP is also subject to activity-dependent post-translational modification(s). This is reflected in transfer of metabolic label from intracellular pools of tritiated adenosine and 32P phosphate onto BiP, covalently modifying the protein (Carlsson and Lazarides, 1983; Hendershot et al., 1988)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Covalent modification of BiP imparts upon it a lower isoelectric point (pI).
source: This is reflected in transfer of metabolic label from intracellular pools of tritiated adenosine and 32P phosphate onto BiP, covalently modifying the protein (Carlsson and Lazarides, 1983; Hendershot et al., 1988) and imparting upon it a lower isoelectric point (pI) (Carlsson and Lazarides, 1983; Laitusis et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Covalent transformation(s) of BiP correlate inversely with the burden of unfolded proteins in the ER.
source: These covalent transformation(s) of BiP correlate inversely with the burden of unfolded proteins in the ER (Chambers et al., 2012; Laitusis et al., 1999; Leno and Ledford, 1989)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The modified form of BiP was under-represented in complex with substrates.
source: and because the modified form of BiP was under-represented in complex with substrates (Hendershot et al., 1988), were deemed to reflect inactivating modification(s) of the chaperone (Chambers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both 32P orthophosphate and 3H adenosine labeling mapped consistently to a cyanogen bromide (CnBr) cleavage fragment in the C-terminal substrate binding domain of BiP (Thr434 to Met541).
source: A consensus emerged in regards to the region of BiP that bears the modification, as both 32P orthophosphate and 3H adenosine labeling mapped consistently to a cyanogen bromide (CnBr) cleavage fragment in the C-terminal substrate binding domain of BiP (Thr434 to Met541) (Chambers et al., 2012; Gaut, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in Arg470 and Arg492 markedly attenuated radiolabeling in vivo of FLAG-tagged BiP expressed in cells.
source: Mutations in two arginine residues on that fragment (Arg470 and Arg492) markedly attenuated radiolabeling in vivo of FLAG-tagged BiP expressed in cells, suggesting that they might be the modification sites (Chambers et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: BiP is subject to AMPylation, which results in the formation of a phosphodiester bond between the alpha phosphate of ATP and a hydroxyl amino acid side chain.
source: Recently it has been reported that BiP is subject to a different modification, AMPylation, which results in the formation of an phosphodiester bond between the alpha phosphate of ATP and a hydroxyl amino acid side chain (with release of pyrophosphate).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: BiP AMPylation is effected by FICD (also known as HYPE).
source: This modification of BiP is effected by a broadly conserved, ER-localized enzyme, FICD (also known as HYPE) (Ham et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: The Orth lab provides evidence that AMPylation is an inactivation modification, induced when client protein burden is low.
source: There is lack of unanimity in regards to the circumstances and consequences of BiP AMPylation: the Orth lab provides evidence that AMPylation is an inactivation modification, induced when client protein burden is low (Ham et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The Mattoo lab suggests that BiP AMPylation is an activating modification induced by ER stress.
source: whereas the Mattoo lab suggests that it is an activating modification induced by ER stress (Sanyal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of protein synthesis led to accumulation of a prominent high mobility species tentatively named 'B' form of BiP.
source: Inhibition of protein synthesis led to accumulation of a prominent high mobility species tentatively named 'B' form
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Depletion of ER calcium progressively drew on the pool of 'B' form BiP to promote the assembly of BiP oligomers.
source: whereas depletion of ER calcium progressively drew on this pool to promote the assembly of BiP oligomers (Preissler et al., 2015) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The 'B' form of BiP was relatively resistant to cleavage in vitro by SubA protease.
source: The 'B' form of BiP was also noted for its relative resistance to cleavage in vitro by a bacterial protease, SubA, which cuts BiP within a highly conserved linker sequence connecting the nucleotide binding domain (NBD) and substrate binding domain (SBD) (Paton et al., 2006) (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Resistance to cleavage by SubA is a feature of the acidic, modified form of BiP.
source: Resistance to cleavage by SubA is also a feature of the acidic, modified form of BiP (Chambers et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The SubA-resistant 'B' form, prominent in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells, was conspicuously absent in FICD-/- cells.
source: The SubA-resistant 'B' form, prominent in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells, was conspicuously absent in FICD-/- cells (compare lanes 2 and 5 in Figure 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FICD inactivation led to disappearance of the acidic form of BiP present in lysates of cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells resolved by isoelectric focusing PAGE.
source: FICD inactivation also led to disappearance of the acidic form of BiP, present in lysates of cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells resolved by isoelectric focusing PAGE (IEF-PAGE, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutation of glutamate 234 to glycine (FICDE234G) de-represses FICD.
source: FICD-mediated AMPylation is strongly autoinhibited by intramolecular competition for ATP γ-phosphate binding by glutamate 234, whose mutation to glycine (FICDE234G) de-represses FICD
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Replacement of histidine 363 with alanine (FICDH363A) abolishes AMPylation activity.
source: whereas replacement of histidine 363, which is located in the highly conserved catalytic FIC motif, with alanine (FICDH363A) abolishes AMPylation activity (Engel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Enforced overexpression of the constitutively active FICDE234G led to the re-appearance of an acidic form of BiP in the FICD-/- cells.
source: In keeping with these observations, enforced overexpression of the constitutively active FICDE234G led to the re-appearance of an acidic form of BiP in the FICD-/- cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Wildtype FICD did not promote BiP's acidic form, even when strongly overexpressed.
source: Wildtype FICD did not promote BiP's acidic form, even when strongly overexpressed, suggesting the existence of robust inhibitory mechanisms restraining potentially deleterious effects of protein modification (Engel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and citation to prior work.

claim: A decline in 'B' form and an increase in susceptibility to digestion by SubA were noted within 2 hr of exposure of cells to 2-deoxyglucose.
source: A decline in 'B' form and an increase in susceptibility to digestion by SubA were noted within 2 hr of exposure of cells to the reversible ER stress inducing agent 2-deoxyglucose ( Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Decline in 'B' form occurred in the face of a marked increase in FICD mRNA.
source: This decline in 'B' form occurred in the face of a marked increase in FICD mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Ham et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citations to prior work.

claim: Washout of 2-deoxyglucose was associated with progressive increase in 'B' form and the emergence of resistance to cleavage by SubA.
source: Washout of 2-deoxyglucose was associated with progressive increase in 'B' form and the emergence of resistance to cleavage by SubA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: Active FICDE234G promoted the ATP-dependent in vitro appearance of a 'B' form of recombinant BiP purified from bacteria.
source: Whether purified as a GST-fusion protein from bacteria or from overexpressing mammalian cells, active FICDE234G promoted the ATP-dependent in vitro appearance of a 'B' form of recombinant BiP purified from bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 'B' form constituted in vitro was partially resistant to cleavage by SubA.
source: Like the endogenous 'B' form, found in cells, the 'B' form constituted in vitro was also partially resistant to cleavage by SubA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Emergence of the 'B' form in vitro correlated with the acquisition of a faster migrating acidic form of BiP on IEF-PAGE.
source: Emergence of the 'B' form in vitro correlated with the acquisition of a faster migrating acidic form of BiP on IEF-PAGE (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FICD converted all the detectable BiP to a single acidic form in a time-dependent manner.
source: FICD converted all the detectable BiP to a single acidic form in a time-dependent manner, which, like the endogenous acidic from of BiP, was also relatively resistant to cleavage by SubA (Figure 3B, lane 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Addition of purified active FICDE234G to lysates from FICD-/- cells entirely converted endogenous BiP into the acidic form.
source: Likewise, addition of purified active FICDE234G to lysates from FICD-/- cells entirely converted endogenous BiP into the acidic form (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Within the resolution of IEF-PAGE, there is no evidence for heterogeneity in BiP modification.
source: Of note, within the resolution of IEF-PAGE, there is no evidence for heterogeneity in BiP modification [also see (Carlsson and Lazarides, 1983; Laitusis et al., 1999)].
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citations to prior work.

claim: FICD efficiently transferred the 32P label from the alpha phosphate of ATP onto BiP, consistent with AMPylation.
source: FICD efficiently transferred the 32P label from the alpha phosphate of ATP onto BiP, consistent with AMPylation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cleavage of radiolabeled BiP by SubA led to emergence of a radiolabeled substrate binding domain fragment (Leu417-Leu654).
source: Interestingly, cleavage of radiolabeled BiP (by prolonged incubation with SubA) led to emergence of a radiolabeled substrate binding domain fragment (Leu417-Leu654); the nucleotide binding domain fragment, though conspicuous on the Coomassie-stained gel, was entirely devoid of label (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The nucleotide binding domain fragment of BiP cleaved by SubA was entirely devoid of radioactive label.
source: the nucleotide binding domain fragment, though conspicuous on the Coomassie-stained gel, was entirely devoid of label (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The in vitro labeling pattern fits well with the metabolic labeling of BiP by 32P orthophosphate or 3H adenosine label donors in vivo.
source: This in vitro labeling pattern fits well with the metabolic labeling of BiP by 32P orthophosphate or 3H adenosine label donors in vivo, as the label was mapped to a single CnBr cleavage fragment spanning Thr434 to Met541 (Chambers et al., 2012; Gaut, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: FICD-mediated transfer of 32P label from ATP to BiP's substrate binding domain cannot be reconciled with reported AMPylation of Thr366 or Ser365.
source: In contrast, FICD-mediated transfer of 32P label from ATP to BiP's substrate binding domain, observed here in vitro, can not be reconciled with reported AMPylation of Thr366 or Ser365 (Ham et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on logical inference from the experimental data and comparison with prior reports.

claim: Electrospray ionization mass spectrometry of purified recombinant BiP produced molecular masses of 71,060.1 and 71,395.6 Da for unmodified and modified BiP, respectively.
source: These preparations were examined by electrospray ionization mass spectrometry and produced molecular masses of 71,060.1 and 71,395.6 Da for unmodified and modified BiP, respectively (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mass difference of 335 Da between unmodified and modified BiP is consistent with a single covalent modification by AMP (329.12 Da).
source: The mass difference of 335 Da is consistent with a single covalent modification by AMP (329.12 Da) in modified BiP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on comparison of measured mass difference with expected mass of AMP.

claim: Mass spectrometry of endogenous BiP immunopurified from cycloheximide-treated wildtype CHO-K1 cells revealed only two molecular masses (70,538.3 Da and 70,866.1 Da) with a mass difference of 327.8 Da.
source: An analogous mass spectrometry experiment with endogenous BiP immunopurified from cycloheximide-treated wildtype CHO-K1 cells also revealed only two molecular masses (70,538.3 Da and 70,866.1 Da) with a mass difference of 327.8 Da, consistent with modification of BiP by a single AMP moiety in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: BiP from AMPylation-deficient FICD-/- cells gave rise to a single species with a molecular mass (70,532.2 Da) similar to the predicted mass of unmodified mature BiP.
source: BiP from AMPylation-deficient FICD-/- cells gave rise to a single species with a molecular mass (70,532.2 Da) that is similar to the predicted mass of unmodified mature BiP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A unique peptide (doubly charged peak of 1374.15 m/z) corresponding in mass to an AMPylation of residues 511-532 was observed in samples digested with Arg-C.
source: A unique peptide (doubly charged peak of 1374.15 m/z) corresponding in mass to an AMPylation of residues 511-532 was observed in samples digested with Arg-C
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A peptide (doubly charged peak of 916.94 m/z) corresponding to AMPylation of residues 515-528 was detected in the Asp-N digest.
source: and another peptide (doubly charged peak of 916.94 m/z) corresponding to AMPylation of residues 515-528 was detected in the Asp-N digest (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: A doubly charged peak (1209.62 m/z) corresponding to the unmodified BiP 511-532 fragment was present in the Arg-C digests of unmodified BiP and absent from the spectrum of the modified form.
source: Moreover, another doubly charged peak (1209.62 m/z) corresponding to the unmodified BiP 511-532 fragment was present in the Arg-C digests of unmodified BiP and absent from the spectrum of the modified form (Figure 4C, left panels)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All four digests (chymotrypsin, trypsin, Arg-C, Asp-N) contained peptides covering Ser365 and Thr366, but these were all unmodified peptides.
source: However, all four digests contained peptides covering Ser365 and Thr366, but these were all unmodified peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The specificity of FICD for AMPylation of hydroxyl side chains and the overlap of modified peptides from the two digests narrows the modification site to three residues: Thr518, Thr525 and Thr527.
source: The specificity of FICD for AMPylation of hydroxyl side chains and the overlap of modified peptides from the two digests narrows the modification site to three residues: Thr518, Thr525 and Thr527.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the mass spectrometry data and known FICD specificity.

claim: Both BiPT525A and BiPT527A remained substrates for AMPylation in vitro.
source: Both BiPT525A and BiPT527A remained substrates for AMPylation in vitro, whereas the BiPT518A mutation abolished all modification of BiP (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The BiPT518A mutation abolished all modification of BiP in vitro.
source: Both BiPT525A and BiPT527A remained substrates for AMPylation in vitro, whereas the BiPT518A mutation abolished all modification of BiP (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: BiPT366A, BiPR470E, and BiPR492E were all modified by FICDE234G in vitro with varying efficiency.
source: BiPT366A and BiPR470E or BiPR492E [the latter are mutations that attenuate labeling of FLAG-tagged BiP in vivo by 32P orthophosphate or 3H adenosine (Chambers et al., 2012)] were all modified by FICDE234G in vitro with varying efficiency, as was the substrate binding-deficient mutant BiPV461F (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The substrate binding-deficient mutant BiPV461F was modified by FICDE234G in vitro.
source: as was the substrate binding-deficient mutant BiPV461F (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The substitution of Thr518 by either alanine or glutamic acid moderately impaired the ability of BiP to form oligomers.
source: The substitution of Thr518 by either alanine or glutamic acid moderately impaired the ability of BiP to form oligomers and slightly modified the mobility of the monomeric ('A') form of BiP on native gels
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mutating Thr366 had no effect on BiP oligomerization.
source: whereas mutating Thr366 had no effect on oligomerization (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: BiPT518E could not be AMPylated in vitro.
source: BiPT518E could not be AMPylated in vitro (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: BiPT518E resembled AMPylated BiP by its migration on native-PAGE and by its resistance to SubA-mediated proteolytic cleavage, whether exposed to FICDE234G or not.
source: Yet, whether exposed to FICDE234G or not, BiPT518E resembled AMPylated BiP by its migration on native-PAGE and by its resistance to SubA-mediated proteolytic cleavage (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted and AMPylated BiP511-532 is reciprocally enriched in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells.
source: Note that unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted and AMPylated BiP511-532 is reciprocally enriched in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 6B and is supported by the SILAC data shown in the figure.

claim: Unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted by cycloheximide treatment only in wildtype cells.
source: Note that unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted by cycloheximide treatment only in wildtype cells and AMPylated BiP511-532 is only detected in wildtype cells.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 6C and is supported by the SILAC data shown in the figure.

claim: AMPylated BiP511-532 is only detected in wildtype cells.
source: Note that unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted by cycloheximide treatment only in wildtype cells and AMPylated BiP511-532 is only detected in wildtype cells.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 6C and is supported by the SILAC data shown in the figure.

claim: The fragmentation spectra of Arg-C peptides 511-532 from both endogenous BiP AMPylated in vivo and recombinant BiP AMPylated in vitro yielded a collection of y-ions and b-ions that included all the residues on the 511-532 peptide except Thr518.
source: The fragmentation spectra of Arg-C peptides 511-532 from both endogenous BiP AMPylated in vivo, or recombinant BiP AMPylated in vitro, yielded a collection of y-ions and b-ions that included all the residues on the 511-532 peptide except Thr518, whereas the latter residue was conspicuously represented in the ion series from the fragmentation spectrum of unmodified endogenous and recombinant BiP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Thr518 was conspicuously represented in the ion series from the fragmentation spectrum of unmodified endogenous and recombinant BiP.
source: whereas the latter residue was conspicuously represented in the ion series from the fragmentation spectrum of unmodified endogenous and recombinant BiP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: BiPE201G and BiPT229A exhibited enhanced AMPylation rates compared to wildtype BiP.
source: BiPE201G and BiPT229A, mutants that bind ATP and undergo allosteric transitions but are defective in nucleotide hydrolysis (Gaut and Hendershot, 1993; Petrova et al., 2008; Wei et al., 1995), exhibited enhanced AMPylation rates compared to wildtype BiP (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: BiPT37G showed slightly reduced AMPylation compared to wildtype BiP.
source: By contrast, BiPT37G, which is defective in ATP hydrolysis and in the allosteric transitions upon ATP binding, showed slightly reduced AMPylation
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: BiPG226D and BiPADDA remained unmodified by FICD.
source: whereas mutants that are severely defective in adopting the ATP-bound conformation, such as the ATP binding-deficient BiPG226D or BiPADDA, which is locked in the domain-uncoupled state due to a four residue substitution in its interdomain linker (Laufen et al., 1999; Preissler et al., 2015), remained unmodified by FICD (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The isolated BiP substrate binding domain was not modified by FICDE234G.
source: Consistent with an important role for the conformation of BiP in determining its ability to serve as a substrate for FICD, the isolated BiP substrate binding domain (purified from bacteria as a fusion to yeast Smt3) was not modified by FICDE234G (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The t1/2max values for in vitro AMPylation of BiPT229A (4.0 min) and BiPE201G (2.3 min) were significantly shorter than for wildtype BiP (9.9 min).
source: The t1/2max values for in vitro AMPylation of BiPT229A (4.0 min) and BiPE201G (2.3 min) were significantly shorter than for wildtype BiP (9.9 min) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: AMPylation lowered the basal ATP hydrolysis rate of BiP by ~50%.
source: AMPylation lowered the basal ATP hydrolysis rate of BiP by ~50% (Figure 8A and B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The ATPase activity of unmodified BiP was enhanced by the presence of a J-domain in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: and, while the ATPase activity of unmodified BiP was enhanced by the presence of a J-domain in a concentration-dependent manner, AMPylated BiP was almost entirely resistant to J-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: AMPylated BiP was almost entirely resistant to J-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis.
source: and, while the ATPase activity of unmodified BiP was enhanced by the presence of a J-domain in a concentration-dependent manner, AMPylated BiP was almost entirely resistant to J-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: AMPylation barely influenced steady-state binding of substrate peptide to BiP.
source: AMPylation barely influenced steady-state binding of substrate peptide to BiP: The dissociation constants of the complex between unmodified BiP or AMPylated BiP and a well-characterized substrate peptide, HTFPAVLGSC, measured at equilibrium (in the presence of ADP) by fluorescence polarization, were similar (KdBiP 16.7 µM and KdBiP-AMP 11.5 µM; Figure 8D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Challenge with excess of unlabeled peptide revealed a markedly higher "off" rate of the complex between AMPylated BiP and the bound peptide (koffBiP 0.037 ± 0.006 min-1 vs. koffBiP-AMP 0.212 ± 0.021 min-1).
source: However, challenge with excess of unlabeled peptide revealed a markedly higher "off" rate of the complex between AMPylated BiP and the bound peptide (koffBiP 0.037 ± 0.006 min-1 vs. koffBiP-AMP 0.212 ± 0.021 min-1; Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Enforced expression of constitutively active FICDE234G led to activation of the CHOP::GFP UPR reporter.
source: The dormant reporter was activated by tunicamycin-induced ER stress (Figure 9A, panels 1 and 2; a positive control), and by acquisition of a constitutively active FICDE234G but not by a catalytically dead FICDE234G-H363A nor by the regulated wildtype enzyme (Figure 9A, panels 3-5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Catalytically dead FICDE234G-H363A did not activate the CHOP::GFP UPR reporter.
source: and by acquisition of a constitutively active FICDE234G but not by a catalytically dead FICDE234G-H363A nor by the regulated wildtype enzyme (Figure 9A, panels 3-5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The regulated wildtype FICD enzyme did not activate the CHOP::GFP UPR reporter.
source: and by acquisition of a constitutively active FICDE234G but not by a catalytically dead FICDE234G-H363A nor by the regulated wildtype enzyme (Figure 9A, panels 3-5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The induction of the UPR reporter in CHO-K1 cells was mirrored by the behavior of endogenous BiP, whose levels increased in a time-dependent manner in human HEK 293 cells upon activation of a conditional allele encoding FICDE234G.
source: The induction of the UPR reporter in CHO-K1 cells was mirrored by the behavior of endogenous BiP, whose levels increased in a time-dependent manner in human HEK 293 cells upon activation of a conditional allele encoding FICDE234G (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Sustained FICDE234G expression had an adverse effect on cell viability.
source: As suggested previously (Sanyal et al., 2015), the capacity of the cells to compensate for the consequences of deregulated FICD activity is limited; reflected here by the adverse effect of sustained FICDE234G expression on cell viability (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: FICD knockout led to a conspicuous temporal delay in PERK and IRE1α autophosphorylation in AR42j cells exposed to DTT.
source: FICD knockout led to a conspicuous temporal delay in PERK and IRE1α autophosphorylation, observed in two independently derived AR42j FICD-/- clones (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Pre-exposure to cycloheximide attenuated subsequent translational repression by DTT-mediated PERK activation in FICD-/- cells.
source: In this experiment, wildtype or FICD-/- AR42j cells were pre-exposed to cycloheximide for 3 hr followed by brief washout to allow recovery of protein synthesis, which was measured by incorporation of puromycin label into newly synthesized proteins. In wildtype cells, DTT led to marked attenuation of protein synthesis, regardless of pre-exposure to cycloheximide (Figure 10E, compare lanes 1 and 2 and 3 and 4), however pre-exposure to cycloheximide attenuated subsequent translational repression by DTT-mediated PERK activation in FICD-/- cells (Figure 10E, lanes 5-8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: FICD deletion had no measureable effect on the kinetics of CHOP::GFP expression induced by treatment with tunicamycin.
source: The aforementioned defect in UPR activation in FICD-/- cells was both fleeting and dependent on the pre-imposition of a low incoming protein flux regime on the ER (attained experimentally by cycloheximide pre-treatment), as FICD deletion had no measureable effect on the kinetics of CHOP::GFP expression induced by treatment with tunicamycin (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: FICD-mediated AMPylation on Thr518 is the major, if not the only covalent change in BiP detectable by existing methods.
source: These findings unify and clarify the pre-existing observations regarding BiP modification and indicate that FICD-mediated AMPylation on Thr518 is the major, if not the only covalent change in this chaperone detectable by the existing methods.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the totality of experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: FICD-mediated AMPylation on Thr518 is sufficient to account for the previously observed key features of modified BiP, namely its acidity and inertness.
source: Furthermore, FICD-mediated AMPylation on Thr518 is sufficient to account for the previously observed key features of modified BiP, namely its acidity and inertness.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Thr518 of hamster BiP is highly conserved in other eukaryotes.
source: Thr518 of hamster BiP is highly conserved in other eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on sequence comparison knowledge.

claim: Mobilization of the Thr518 side chain by allosteric signals attendant upon ATP binding is suggested to enhance exposure of Thr518 to solvent explaining the selective FICD-mediated modification of ATP-bound BiP.
source: Exposure of the Thr518 side chain to the solvent is likely enhanced further by the loss of four other polar interactions that stabilize L7,8 in the ADP state (Yang et al., 2015). Therefore, mobilization of the side chain by allosteric signals attendant upon ATP binding is suggested to enhance exposure of Thr518 to solvent explaining the selective FICD-mediated modification of ATP-bound BiP and the absence of modification of mutant variants of BiP that are defective in domain coupling (BiPADDA, BiPG226D and to a lesser extent BiPT37G).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on structural analysis and inference from experimental data.

claim: BiP in the compact ATP-bound conformation is the preferred substrate for FICD.
source: Together, these observations indicate that modification of BiP is modulated by its conformation and BiP in the compact ATP-bound conformation is the preferred substrate for FICD.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the totality of experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.
